source: Goodman, Mansinghka, Roy, Bonawitz, Tenenbaum (2008) Church: a language for generative models
finding: Church is a stochastic lambda calculus on Scheme. Models are ordinary programs. A query primitive turns sampling into conditional sampling, so any generative program can be conditioned on a predicate.
numbers: Core primitives: flip and other random procedures, mem (stochastic memoisation), query / lex-query. No behavioural experiments in this paper.
limits: Founding language paper, not an empirical test. Query by rejection or MCMC is slow in general.
agent_relevance: Template an agent can copy: write a world model as code, then condition it on evidence. Background only.

source: Wong, Grand, Lew, Goodman, Mansinghka, Andreas, Tenenbaum (2023) From Word Models to World Models (rational meaning construction, PLoT)
finding: Proposes that an LLM translates language into WebPPL/Church-style probabilistic programs and Bayesian inference over the program does the reasoning. Shown in four domains: probabilistic, relational, visual-physical, social reasoning.
numbers: Uses Codex few-shot with comment-code pairs. Illustrative worked examples (tug-of-war domain, etc.). No aggregate accuracy table or human-subject data.
quote: LLMs can generate context-sensitive translations that capture pragmatically-appropriate linguistic meanings
limits: Qualitative demonstrations only; Codex is a 2021-era model.
agent_relevance: Blueprint for a think-in-code loop: LLM writes a model, a probabilistic engine answers the query.

source: Wong, Grand, Lew, Goodman, Mansinghka, Andreas, Tenenbaum (2023) From Word Models to World Models (rational meaning construction, PLoT) - uncertainty wording
finding: Codex maps hedge words to probability values in a sensible range (a propensity phrase versus 'rarely lazy' get different numbers) and reuses the same program structure across paraphrases.
numbers: Shown by example translations in Fig. 4 and appendix; no scored sample.
limits: Anecdotal. Numeric mapping of hedges is not validated against human norms in this paper.
agent_relevance: A way to turn verbal confidence into explicit numbers inside a scaffold, then check them.

source: Wong, Grand, Lew, Goodman, Mansinghka, Andreas, Tenenbaum (2023) From Word Models to World Models (rational meaning construction, PLoT) - building the model itself
finding: Given line-by-line language explaining a tug-of-war game, Codex wrote a generative model from scratch that recovered the essential structure of the hand-coded model, with slightly different priors.
numbers: One domain (tug-of-war), a single worked demonstration.
limits: No repeated-run statistics.
agent_relevance: Suggests the LLM can draft the world model, not only fill query slots. Needs a verification step.

source: Lew, Zhi-Xuan, Grand, Mansinghka (2023) Sequential Monte Carlo Steering of LLMs using Probabilistic Programs (LLaMPPL)
finding: Introduces LLaMPPL, a probabilistic programming library where a LLaMA model is a random choice inside a program. SMC steering clones promising particles and culls bad ones during generation, with caching of neural activations across particles.
numbers: Feynman-Kac Transformer model; expansion factor K=3; mean log Z estimate over 10 runs rises with number of particles N (Fig. 4, prompt-intersection task).
limits: Demonstrations on constrained generation, prompt intersection, infilling. Few benchmark accuracy numbers in this first paper.
agent_relevance: Cleanest example of a probabilistic program that wraps an LLM and reallocates compute mid-generation.

source: Lew, Zhi-Xuan, Grand, Mansinghka (2023) Sequential Monte Carlo Steering of LLMs using Probabilistic Programs (LLaMPPL) - versus locally constrained decoding
finding: Token-masking decoding can distort the distribution. SMC with potentials tends to the true constrained posterior as particles grow, and E[log Z] lower-bounds log Z.
numbers: Theory plus Fig. 4 (10 runs, N varied).
limits: Needs LLM token probabilities, so closed chat APIs without logits cannot be used.
agent_relevance: Limits use with closed models behind chat APIs.

source: Loula et al. (2025) Syntactic and Semantic Control of LLMs via Sequential Monte Carlo (ICLR 2025)
finding: SMC with grammar constraints plus a semantic potential lets small open models beat bigger ones on four tasks: goal inference (Planetarium PDDL), molecule synthesis, DS-1000 Python, Spider text-to-SQL.
numbers: N=10 particles. Base LM vs Full SMC score: goal inference 0.063 to 0.419; molecules 0.132 to 0.577; text-to-SQL 0.531 to 0.620; data science 0.213 base to 0.346 or 0.407 (two Full SMC cells in the garbled table).
limits: Data-science row is garbled in text extraction; check the paper table before quoting a single cell. Gains from weight correction are small.
agent_relevance: Probabilistic-programming inference over an LLM gives large measured gains, mostly from resampling plus a task-specific check.

source: Loula et al. (2025) Syntactic and Semantic Control of LLMs via Sequential Monte Carlo (ICLR 2025) - ablation and compute
finding: Full SMC matches or beats Full importance sampling with one tenth of the particles in 3 of 4 domains. On goal inference: grammar-only SMC 0.401, Sample-Rerank 0.289, Full IS 0.257, Full SMC 0.419.
numbers: Molecular: Full IS 0.404, Full SMC 0.577, grammar-only SMC 0.205. Goal inference base 0.063 vs grammar constraint alone 0.086.
limits: Benefit depends on the expensive semantic potential; grammar alone helps little.
agent_relevance: Check partial work early and resample beats generate-then-filter.

source: Loula et al. (2025) Syntactic and Semantic Control of LLMs via Sequential Monte Carlo (ICLR 2025) - Llama 3.1 70B versus Codex
finding: Llama 3.1 70B with Full SMC outperforms Codex-002 (175B, code fine-tuned) on DS-1000. Small models also outperform models over 8 times larger in 3 of 4 domains.
numbers: Main-text summary bullets (Fig. 2, Tables 2 and 4).
limits: Codex-002 numbers taken from Lai et al. 2023.
agent_relevance: Inference-time structure can replace model size on narrow tasks.

source: Grand, Pepe, Andreas, Tenenbaum (2024) Loose LIPS Sink Ships: Battleship question-asking with language-informed program sampling (CogSci 2024)
finding: Pipeline: LLM proposes natural-language questions, translates them to Battleship DSL programs, scores each by expected information gain (EIG) under a probabilistic world model. A few samples reach human-level questions.
numbers: 18 boards, human data from Rothe et al. Human mean EIG 1.27, best human 3.61, 97% of human questions informative. Single samples (k=1) averaged EIG about 0.65-0.66 (CodeLlama-7b, GPT-4); grammar baseline 0.36. At k=5 near human mean; at k=10 both beat human mean (p<0.001 CodeLlama, p=0.01 GPT-4).
limits: Best human questions (about 85-90th percentile) were not matched. Limited to the Battleship DSL.
agent_relevance: Strong case for sample-then-score with an explicit probabilistic model: about 10 cheap samples replace expertise.

source: Grand, Pepe, Andreas, Tenenbaum (2024) Loose LIPS Sink Ships: Battleship question-asking with language-informed program sampling (CogSci 2024) - translation fidelity
finding: Few-shot translation into programs worked 75% (CodeLlama) and 88% (GPT-4). GPT-4 zero-shot translated only 40% and defaulted to boolean questions.
numbers: Percentages from the prose of the translation-fidelity section.
limits: Table 1 cells are garbled in extraction; figures here come from the prose.
agent_relevance: Few-shot examples matter a lot for code translation.

source: Grand, Pepe, Andreas, Tenenbaum (2024) Loose LIPS Sink Ships: Battleship question-asking with language-informed program sampling (CogSci 2024) - grounding failure of pure LLMs
finding: LLM-only baselines struggle to ground questions in the board. GPT-4V gave no improvement over non-visual baselines, and GPT-4 with no board shown scored about the same EIG as with the board.
numbers: k=1 EIG about 0.65 few-shot with board, about 0.66 with no board (from Table 1 and text).
limits: Reading from a partly garbled table.
agent_relevance: Pure LLM questioning ignores state; scoring against a world model injects the grounding.

source: Ellis (2023) Human-like Few-Shot Learning via Bayesian Reasoning over Natural Language (NeurIPS 2023)
finding: A GPT-4 proposal distribution writes candidate concepts in English, which are reweighted by a prior and likelihood. Tuned on human data it fits the Number Game closely with 50-100 proposals.
numbers: Number Game: tuned prior R2=0.95 at 100 samples against 8 human raters; the original Number Game model used over 5000 hypotheses. Raw GPT-4 yes/no probabilities were decidedly different from humans.
limits: Average over only 8 raters. English hypotheses beat Python hypotheses; ablating the data-conditioned proposal gives a poor fit.
agent_relevance: LLM hypothesis proposal plus explicit Bayes re-weighting is a usable scaffold; plain-language hypotheses beat code.

source: Ellis (2023) Human-like Few-Shot Learning via Bayesian Reasoning over Natural Language (NeurIPS 2023) - logical concepts
finding: On 112 logical concepts with 1,596 human participants, the model explained 81% of variance in human responses with 100 proposals per batch and was within 3% of human accuracy.
numbers: R2=0.81; classic Bayesian program learning needed about 10^9 proposals (about 45,000 unique concepts) and fit slightly worse.
limits: Tuning the prior was critical; model slightly underperforms humans.
agent_relevance: About seven orders of magnitude fewer proposals than classic MCMC program search.

source: Ying, Zhi-Xuan, Wong, Mansinghka, Tenenbaum (2023) The Neuro-Symbolic Inverse Planning Engine (NIPE)
finding: LLM translates language into a symbolic goal-inference model; Bayesian inverse planning computes posteriors. Compared with GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 asked to rate directly.
numbers: n=46 participants (6 excluded). Model vs humans R=0.927 (95% CI 0.877-0.953). GPT-4 rating R=0.658 (CI 0.403-0.79). GPT-3.5 R=0.100 (CI -0.145 to 0.361).
limits: GPT-4 near zero on the Colored-Different rule variant and weak on spatial path planning; gridworld key puzzles only.
agent_relevance: LLM as translator plus Bayesian engine beats LLM as direct judge on novel rules.

source: Ying, Zhi-Xuan, Wong, Mansinghka, Tenenbaum (2024) Grounding Language about Belief in a Bayesian Theory-of-Mind
finding: Belief sentences are translated into epistemic formulas and evaluated by a Bayesian theory-of-mind model over agent goals and beliefs, matching human ratings in a doors-and-keys puzzle.
numbers: 100 Prolific participants, 18 scenarios. Full BToM vs humans r=0.93 (goals), r=0.92 and 0.86 for the two belief-prior variants. Omniscient observer r=0.64; heuristic and non-mentalizer baselines r about 0.04-0.19.
limits: Assumes deterministic beliefs. Which table row has which prior is ambiguous in the text extraction.
agent_relevance: Modelling the other agent's mind inside a program beats surface heuristics.

source: Collins, Wong, Feng, Wei, Tenenbaum (2022) Structured, flexible, and robust: benchmarking LLMs on out-of-distribution reasoning
finding: On novel planning and explanation prompts with constrained answers, GPT-3 scored below humans in every condition. A Parse-and-Solve hybrid (Codex parse to PDDL plus symbolic planner) did better on constrained planning.
numbers: 240 human generators; blind raters N=393 on a 7-point scale; humans beat GPT-3 in all conditions (p<0.001). In the most constrained planning condition the LLM-as-planner solved none of the problems.
limits: Small design; LLM and hybrid declined similarly with constraints (no significant interaction), partly a floor effect. GPT-3 and Codex, 2022.
agent_relevance: Early evidence that an LLM parser plus structured solver is more robust off-distribution than an LLM alone.

source: Zhi-Xuan, Ying, Mansinghka, Tenenbaum (2024) Pragmatic Instruction Following via Cooperative Language-Guided Inverse Planning (CLIPS)
finding: A Bayesian agent infers a human's goal from actions and ambiguous language, then helps. Beats GPT-4V, literal instruction following and action-only inverse planning.
numbers: CLIPS 1.26 to 1.68 times faster at reaching the human's goal than baselines and 1.18 to 1.58 times less costly. Human-rating correlations per panel range r=0.15 to 0.96.
limits: Gridworld and VirtualHome style domains; wide range of r means fit is uneven.
agent_relevance: Probabilistic goal inference gives pragmatic help that raw multimodal LLMs miss.

source: Wong, Collins, Ying, Zhang, Weller, Gerstenberg, O'Donnell, Lew, Andreas, Tenenbaum, Brooke-Wilson (2025) Modeling Open-World Cognition as On-Demand Synthesis of Probabilistic Models (CogSci 2025)
finding: Model Synthesis Architecture: Llama-3.1-70B builds an ad hoc WebPPL model for each question, with Bayesian inference over it. Compared with LM-direct and LM-CoT baselines and hand-written gold models on sports reasoning vignettes.
numbers: Three human experiments; 1000 posterior samples (Exp 1-2) or 500 (Exp 3) per simulated participant; humans gave 5 judgments per question. MSA fit stayed within the 95% CI of the human split-half baseline; LM-only baselines fit worse, most in open-world Exp 3.
limits: MSA samples varied too little (lower variance than people, canoe domain especially). Authors say stronger baselines and ablations are needed; no single headline r in main text.
agent_relevance: A PPL-based loop fits human graded judgments better than direct or CoT prompting when the situation is novel.

source: Wong, Collins, Ying, Zhang, Weller, Gerstenberg, O'Donnell, Lew, Andreas, Tenenbaum, Brooke-Wilson (2025) Modeling Open-World Cognition as On-Demand Synthesis of Probabilistic Models (CogSci 2025) - LLM-only baseline failures
finding: LM-only baselines were less coherent across related variables and diverged from people more as stimuli grew more novel, consistent with Collins et al. 2022.
numbers: Described in Key finding 1 and Fig. 7 (cross-model R2 blocks); values are in the paper figures, not extracted here.
limits: No numbers extracted.
agent_relevance: Coherence across linked questions is what a joint program provides and separate prompts do not.

source: Li, Fox, Goodman (2024) Automated Statistical Model Discovery with Language Models (BoxLM)
finding: GPT-4 loop in the style of Box's loop: a proposer writes probabilistic programs (PyMC), a critic reads posterior-predictive checks and suggests changes. 4 rounds, 12 proposals per round, proposal temperature 0.7, critic temperature 0.
numbers: Leave-one-out ELPD vs expert programs: Eight schools -30.42 vs -30.70; Dugongs 23.40 vs 22.52; Surgical -38.03 vs -40.29; Peregrine -173.11 vs -142.19 (worse). Metadata removed, Surgical sim -63.72 vs expert -39.80.
limits: Peregrine and no-metadata Surgical are clear failures. Only 78% (GPT-4 text), 70% (vision only) and 76% (GPT-3.5) of programs could be scored.
agent_relevance: Complete example of a PPL inside an LLM propose-critique loop, with a failure rate near one in four.

source: Li, Fox, Goodman (2024) Automated Statistical Model Discovery with Language Models (BoxLM) - ablations
finding: GPT-4 shown only plots did about as well as GPT-4 with text; GPT-3.5 was comparable on most datasets.
numbers: ELPD: Surgical GPT-4 text -37.36, visual -38.54, GPT-3.5 -42.2; Peregrine text -164.69, visual -143.45, GPT-3.5 -161.14, expert -142.19.
limits: Only four datasets.
agent_relevance: A cheaper model may be enough in a critique loop.

source: Kanda, Ugare, Misailovic (2026) RefineStat: Efficient Exploration for Probabilistic Program Synthesis (ICLR 2026 oral)
finding: Semantic validity checks during decoding of PyMC code, plus resampling of priors or likelihood when diagnostics (Rhat, ESS, divergences, Pareto-k) fail. Four 7-8B models: Llama3-8B, CodeGemma-7B, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B.
numbers: Run rate (program samples the posterior): Standard 0.10-0.11, SynCode 0.21, RefineStat 0.45-0.50 across temperatures 0.2-0.4. Run rate more than doubles for NumPyro too. ELPD-LOO with DQ-7B: Eight schools -30.68 vs expert -30.70.
limits: Uses about twice the tokens of baseline; DQ-7B much worse on Dugongs (8.35 vs 22.43) and Surgical (-114.29 vs -39.73).
agent_relevance: Unconstrained small models mostly fail to produce runnable probabilistic programs; a Bayesian-workflow check loop fixes about half.

source: Kanda, Ugare, Misailovic (2026) RefineStat: Efficient Exploration for Probabilistic Program Synthesis (ICLR 2026 oral) - versus o3 and BoxLM
finding: On Peregrine, RefineStat beats both BoxLM and OpenAI o3; on the GP task it beats o3; elsewhere comparable or somewhat worse.
limits: Row alignment in the table extraction is uncertain for some cells; check the paper.
agent_relevance: Diagnostics-driven repair can substitute for model size when writing models.

source: Huang (2025) LLM-BI: Towards Fully Automated Bayesian Inference with Large Language Models
finding: Gemini 2.5 turned verbal beliefs into PyMC priors and, in a second experiment, wrote a whole Bayesian linear regression model from one problem description.
numbers: Exp I: posteriors from manual weak priors N(0,100), N(0,50), HalfNormal(50) and from LLM-elicited priors were nearly identical. One model class only.
limits: Proof of concept, single simple regression, no benchmark or error rate.
agent_relevance: Prior elicitation by an LLM is easy for simple models. Not evidence for hard cases.

source: Large Language Bayes (2025), secondary summary only
finding: LLM generates many Stan-style models, runs inference on each and averages them with weights.
numbers: A secondary summary reports up to 71.9% valid generated models on a city-temperature problem.
limits: Not verified against the primary paper.
agent_relevance: Model averaging over LLM-written programs hedges against one wrong model.

source: AI4BayesCode (2026), search listing only
finding: System that turns natural-language Bayesian descriptions into validated MCMC samplers, with its own benchmark suite.
numbers: None read.
limits: Only title and abstract seen in search results.
agent_relevance: Worth reading next for benchmark numbers.

source: BLInD dataset (AAAI 2025), search listing only
finding: Reported (secondary) that program-aided methods (PAL, Monte Carlo, ProbLog) improve LLM probabilistic reasoning over text, but PAL struggles on larger Bayesian networks.
numbers: None read.
limits: Secondary summary only.
